tier_reason: Upgraded from C to B. The primary peer-reviewed paper is now in hand (Tyunyayev, Piraux, Bonaventure, Barbette, 'A High-Speed QUIC Implementation', ACM CoNEXT-SW '22; open-access copy on UCLouvain DIAL). Its evaluation says 'Compared to the original picoquic implementation, we see a 3x improvement' in single-connection goodput on two Xeon Silver 4314 machines over a 100 Gbps link. It is not A: the public NPF harness (UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk-experiments, repo/*.repo and quic_tester_compare.npf) exists, but no compiler or flags are stated; the builds are a plain 'cmake . && make'.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Primary paper: "Compared to the original picoquic implementation, we see a 3x improvement" in single-connection goodput (abstract: "improving the throughput by a 3x factor"). For handshakes with 0-byte requests, picoquic-dpdk handles up to 6000 requests/s while picoquic manages about half that. The paper also says picoquic-dpdk on 1 core beats quiche, quicly and msquic; msquic reaches 10.6 Gbps with a 3-core pipeline.
corrections.workload: One QUIC connection downloading 20 GB (a picoTLS TCP+TLS reference ran a 30 s download) between a client and a server over a 100 Gbps link. AES-128-GCM for all stacks; no disk I/O. picoquic-dpdk ran on 1 core for both I/O and processing, against kernel-socket stacks (original picoquic, quiche, quicly, msquic) in 1-core and 2-core-pipeline setups. A separate test measured handshake rate with 0-byte requests.
corrections.hardware: Two Intel Xeon Silver 4314 CPUs @ 2.4 GHz (client and server) on a 100 Gbps link; the NIC model is not stated in the paper.
corrections.caveats: The primary paper confirms the 3x figure against plain kernel-socket picoquic, measured with one connection, one core and a 20 GB download on a 100 Gbps link. Compiler and flags are not stated. The paper names https://github.com/UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk as the official code (MIT, 3 stars, last commit 2022-10-31), with scripts in UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk-experiments (NPF, no license). This IPNetworkingLab repo is the earlier master's-thesis version (last commit 2022-06-01), so the paper's numbers may belong to the ENSG repo rather than this one. The repo is not a GitHub-network fork: it is a copied derivative of private-octopus/picoquic. Jaeger et al. (arXiv:2309.16395, IFIP Networking 2023) say they 'are not able to reach similar goodput as reported by Tyunyayev et al.' for picoquic and could not easily reproduce the optimizations. DPDK needs dedicated NIC queues and busy-polling cores, and the paper is a 3-page student-workshop paper.
